title: THE AI DICTIONARY
subtitle: A Practical Reference for Modern AI Systems

terms.definition: Computational systems that can perform functions associated with intelligence, such as prediction, learning, reasoning, perception, planning, generation, or decision support.

Hypothetical broad, flexible, transferable intelligence that can perform most cognitive work at roughly human level or better, including on unfamiliar tasks. No consensus threshold or accepted demonstration exists.
Hypothetical capability substantially beyond the best humans across virtually all cognitive domains.
AI without demonstrated general intelligence. Classic ANI is task-specific, but modern foundation models are general-purpose across many tasks while still not AGI.
Systems that can learn patterns from data instead of being explicitly programmed.
Machine learning using multi-layer neural networks.
Computing model inspired by biological neurons; a large class of modern AI is built on neural networks.
Large model trained on broad data and adaptable to many downstream tasks.
AI that can create new content such as text, images, audio, or video.

A model is the trained computational artifact that maps inputs to outputs. An AI system is the deployed socio-technical product around it: models, data, prompts, retrieval, tools, code, infrastructure, interfaces, policies, monitoring, and human actors.
Training a model on labeled input-output pairs so it can map new inputs to predicted outputs.
Training a model to find structure in unlabeled data, such as clusters or compressed representations.
Training that creates supervisory signals from the data itself, such as predicting masked tokens or nearby views.
Training that combines a small labeled set with a larger unlabeled set.
Reusing knowledge learned on one task to improve performance on a related task.
Learning useful internal features automatically rather than hand-engineering them.
A neural network trained on massive text that can understand and generate language.
The dominant neural architecture, introduced in 2017, based on self-attention.
Autoregressive LLM family (vendor-specific: OpenAI).
Bidirectional encoder model (vendor-specific: Google) used mainly for understanding tasks.
Generative model that denoises random noise into images, audio, or other signals.
Probabilistic generative model that learns a latent distribution and can sample from it.
Two networks competing: a generator that creates samples and a discriminator that tries to detect fakes.
Sequence model that can carry memory of previous inputs through recurrent connections.
RNN variants with gating that can handle longer-range dependencies better than vanilla RNNs.
Grid-pattern model using spatial filters; historically dominant for images.
Architecture that activates only some specialized sub-networks per input.
A model that can handle text, image, audio, and/or video together.
A compact LLM designed to run on edge or phone hardware.
OpenAI's test-time-compute model family (vendor-specific), trained with RL on verifiable tasks.
Open reasoning model family from DeepSeek (vendor-specific), notable for a public training methodology.
Architecture that applies a Transformer directly to sequences of image patches.
Sequence architecture such as Mamba that models dynamics with state-space updates rather than full attention.
RNN-style architecture that aims to match Transformer quality with linear-time inference (vendor-specific lineage).
Chunk of text — a word, subword, character, or symbol — that a language model processes.
Tool that splits text into subword units using a model-specific vocabulary. Designs include byte-level BPE, WordPiece, and Unigram; there is no universal first-256-token layout.
The full list of tokens a model knows.
Numeric vector representing a token, word, or other item in a learned meaning space.
Mechanism letting tokens weigh each other's importance when computing a representation.
Maximum number of tokens a model can consider at once.
Running a trained model to produce outputs.
The learned numbers that define a model's behavior.
Further training on specific data to specialize a model.
Compressing a larger model's knowledge into a smaller one.
Reducing numeric precision to shrink models, for example from FP16 to INT4.
Sampling setting: low values make output more predictable; high values make it more varied.
Methods that limit which tokens can be chosen next by probability mass or rank.
Exploring multiple output paths in parallel to find a high-scoring sequence.
Raw scores for each possible next token, before they are converted to probabilities.
Function that converts logits into a probability distribution.
Measure of error the model learns to minimize.
Algorithm that computes gradients so weights can be adjusted based on error.
Optimization that steps downhill on the loss surface.
One full pass through the training data.
Number of samples processed together in one training or inference step.
Step size of weight updates during training.
Memorizing training data so the model fails to generalize to new inputs.
Techniques that reduce overfitting by constraining model complexity or training dynamics.
Randomly disabling neurons during training as a regularization method.
Controlling which tokens can attend to which others, used for causality, padding, or sparsity.
The residual pathway through a Transformer where layer outputs are added back to the running representation.
Normalizing activations within a layer to stabilize training.
Nonlinear transform such as ReLU, GELU, or sigmoid applied to neuron outputs.
Signal that gives a model information about token order, since attention itself is permutation-sensitive.
Stored attention keys and values from previous tokens, reused to speed autoregressive generation.
Rotary positional embeddings that encode relative position by rotating query and key vectors.
Attention variant that shares key/value heads across groups of query heads to reduce memory.
Attention variant where all query heads share a single key/value head.
IO-aware attention algorithm that computes exact attention with less memory movement.
Empirical pattern where models keep attending strongly to initial tokens, relevant to long-context stability.
The text, images, audio, or other examples a model learns from.
A body of text used for training or evaluation.
Collection, cleaning, formatting, and delivery of training data.
Artificially expanding training data with variations of existing examples.
Initial broad training on massive data before specialization.
Alignment and specialization stages after pre-training, such as SFT and preference optimization.
Training on labeled example responses to teach a desired style or skill.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: using human preference rewards to shape model behavior.
Preference training in which rewards come from an AI judge rather than direct human labels.
Saved snapshot of model weights during or after training.
Total training tokens processed; a core measure of training scale.
Empirical relationships between model size, data, compute, and performance.
Capabilities that appear abruptly in some measurements as models scale; whether these are genuine discontinuities or artifacts of benchmark thresholds remains debated.
Delayed generalization that can appear long after a model has memorized the training set.
Training a model or system jointly from raw inputs to final outputs through the full processing stack.
Machine-generated examples used to expand or replace collected training data.
Choosing model size and data volume to get the best result for a given compute budget.
Loss of previously learned behavior when a model is trained on new tasks.
A change between training conditions and deployment conditions that can degrade performance.
Degradation that can occur when models are repeatedly trained on their own synthetic outputs. Mechanisms and severity are actively studied.
Low-rank adaptation: a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that trains small adapter matrices instead of all weights.
Quantized LoRA: fine-tuning a quantized base model with low-rank adapters.
A parameter-efficient method that learns prefix vectors prepended to activations rather than changing all weights.
Small trainable modules inserted into a frozen model to specialize it with few extra parameters.
Fine-tuning a model on instruction-response pairs so it follows natural-language requests.
Information-theoretic measure of uncertainty in a distribution.
Loss that measures how well predicted probabilities match true labels; standard for classification and language modeling.
Asymmetric measure of how one probability distribution diverges from another.
How well a model's stated confidence matches empirical correctness.
Adaptive optimizers widely used in deep learning; AdamW decouples weight decay from the adaptive update.
Optimizer that uses sign-based updates; used in some large-model training recipes.
Newer optimizer variant explored for large-model training (emerging, not a universal standard).
Geometry of the loss surface over parameter space.
Tension between underfitting from overly simple assumptions and overfitting from excessive sensitivity to training data.
Property of an objective that has no local minima other than the global minimum; useful but uncommon in deep nets.
Ways of measuring vector size and closeness, including L2 distance and cosine similarity.
Keeping computations from overflowing, underflowing, or accumulating destructive rounding error.
Plan for changing the step size over training, such as warmup and cosine decay.
Iterative algorithm for estimating parameters when some variables are latent.
Updating beliefs about unknowns by combining a prior with observed evidence.
Choosing parameters that make the observed data most probable under the model.
Rule-based program designed to simulate the judgment of a human expert in a bounded domain.
Repository of facts, rules, and relations used by a symbolic reasoner.
Component that applies logical rules to a knowledge base to derive conclusions.
Formal specification of concepts and relationships in a domain.
IF-THEN rules used to model stepwise reasoning.
Difficulty of specifying what does not change after an action in a logical world model.
Graph representation of concepts and the relations among them.
Stereotyped event sequences used in classical AI to represent everyday situations.
W3C effort to make web data machine-readable through shared standards and ontologies.
Solving problems by finding assignments that satisfy a set of constraints.
Solving a problem by exploring states and the transitions between them.
Search guided by an estimate of remaining cost or distance to a goal.
Pathfinding algorithm that combines actual path cost with a heuristic estimate of remaining cost.
Adversarial decision rule that minimizes possible loss in a worst-case, typically zero-sum, game tree.
Search optimization that skips minimax branches that cannot affect the final decision.
Search guided by randomized rollouts and statistical tree updates, famously used in AlphaGo.
Classical symbolic planning formalism based on operators with preconditions and effects.
Layered representation of reachable actions and propositions used in classical planning.
Encoding planning problems as satisfiability or satisfiability-modulo-theories instances.
Keeping only the top-k partial paths at each step to trade completeness for speed in planning.
Linear model for classification that outputs class probabilities.
Probabilistic classifier that assumes features are conditionally independent given the class.
Instance-based method that classifies a point from its nearest labeled neighbors.
Interpretable model that splits data with sequential tests on features.
Ensemble of decision trees whose votes or averages form the prediction.
Sequential ensemble method that adds weak learners to correct remaining error.
Classifier that finds a maximum-margin hyperplane between classes.
Grouping unlabeled examples by similarity, as in k-means.
Projecting data into fewer dimensions while preserving structure, as in PCA or t-SNE.
Evaluating a model by rotating held-out splits of the data.
Manually constructing input variables that make a learning problem easier.
Probabilistic graphical model of variables and conditional dependencies on a directed acyclic graph.
Model of a Markov process whose states are not directly observed.
Framework for sequential decisions where outcomes are partly random and partly controlled.
Probabilistic model whose dependence structure is represented as a graph.
Writing probabilistic models as programs and inferring their latent variables.
Quantifying how unsure a model is, including aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty.
Nonparametric Bayesian model over functions, used for regression with uncertainty.
Early neural classifier (1958) computing a weighted sum plus a threshold.
Layered network without recurrent connections; information flows input to output.
Architecture with skip connections that ease training of very deep networks.
Encoder-decoder convolutional architecture widely used for segmentation and as a diffusion backbone.
Network trained to reconstruct its input through a compressed latent code.
Compressed internal representation space in which similar items lie close together.
Learning representations by pulling related examples together and pushing unrelated ones apart.
Learning a similarity space in which distance reflects task-relevant likeness.
Contrastive image-text model (vendor-specific: OpenAI) that embeds images and captions in a shared space.
Interpretability technique that reads intermediate Transformer states as if they were final logits.
Splitting individual layers across chips so one model layer is computed in parallel.
Splitting sequential layers across chips and overlapping their computation.
Replicating a model across chips and splitting the batch.
Sharded-optimizer and fully sharded data-parallel methods that split optimizer state and parameters across devices.
Recomputing activations during backward pass to save memory.
Sudden jump in training loss that can destabilize a run.
Splitting a stream of text into words, subwords, or symbols.
Reducing words to a stem by crude rules (stemming) or to a dictionary lemma (lemmatization).
Locating and classifying names of people, organizations, places, and similar entities in text.
Labeling each word with its grammatical category given context.
Analyzing the grammatical structure of a sentence.
Statistic reflecting how important a term is to a document relative to a corpus.
Predictive embedding method (skip-gram or CBOW) that learns word vectors from local context.
Embedding method that factorizes global word-word co-occurrence statistics.
Predicting the next token or a missing span of text.
Encoder-decoder setup that maps one sequence to another, used for translation and similar tasks.
Automatically converting text from one language to another.
Compressing a document into a shorter text that preserves key meaning.
Returning an answer to a natural-language question, extractive or generative.
Obeying natural-language directions, often measured with verifiable constraints.
Reusing computed prefixes of a prompt so repeated context is cheaper and faster.
Observed tendency of long-context models to underuse information placed in the middle of a prompt.
Informal name for quality drop as a conversation or prompt grows long and noisy.
Subword tokenization that starts from bytes and learns merges; can encode arbitrary text, though not always efficiently.
Subword tokenization used by BERT-style models, with a different vocabulary construction than byte-level BPE.
Subword model that selects a vocabulary by probabilistic unigram language modeling.
Assigning a categorical label to an entire image.
Localizing instances of object classes, typically with bounding boxes.
Labeling every pixel with a class.
Separating individual object instances, even of the same class.
Overlap metric comparing a predicted box or mask with ground truth.
Extracting machine-readable text from images of documents or scenes.
Inferring the pose of a body or object from images or video.
Estimating apparent motion between video frames.
Diffusion process run in a compressed latent space rather than on raw pixels.
Diffusion Transformer: a transformer backbone used inside diffusion models.
Generating images from a text prompt.
Generating moving imagery from a text prompt.
Converting spoken audio into text.
Generating speech audio from text.
Searching one modality using a query from another, such as images from text.
Shared vector space for more than one modality.
Learned compressor for audio or video used as tokens or latents for generative models.
Learning to act by interacting with an environment to maximize cumulative reward.
Mapping from states to actions, or to a distribution over actions.
Estimate of expected future reward from a state or state-action pair.
Recursive relationship between a state's value, its immediate reward, and the value of the next state.
Off-policy algorithm that learns action values without requiring the behavior policy to match the target.
Directly optimizing a policy by following the gradient of expected reward.
RL method that learns both a policy (actor) and a value function (critic).
Trying uncertain actions to gather information, as opposed to exploiting current knowledge.
Exploration rule that usually takes the best-known action and otherwise acts randomly.
Bandit algorithm that prefers actions with high estimated value or high uncertainty.
Internal rewards such as curiosity used when external rewards are sparse.
Modifying the reward signal to make learning easier, at the risk of changing the true objective.
Imitation learning that treats expert trajectories as supervised data.
Performance drop when a policy trained in simulation is deployed in the physical world.
Varying simulation parameters so a policy is more robust when transferred to reality.
A human remotely controlling a robot, often to collect demonstrations.
Model that maps visual observations and language instructions to robot actions.
An agent that acts through a physical or simulated body rather than only through text.
Retrieving relevant external information at query time and supplying it to a model so the response can be grounded in that information.
Keyword-based retrieval such as BM25 that matches terms rather than vectors.
Retrieval that embeds queries and documents into a vector space and searches by similarity.
Combining sparse and dense retrieval, often with a later re-ranker.
Fast, approximate search for vectors near a query, trading a little recall for speed.
Graph-based ANN index used by many vector databases.
System specialized for storing, indexing, and querying embeddings.
A second-stage model that reorders retrieved candidates more carefully.
Connecting an output to supplied, retrieved, or verified evidence rather than relying only on model parameters.
Checking that a cited source actually supports the precise claim attached to it.
Storing past interactions or facts so they can be used in later steps.
A system that combines a model with state, tools, policies, and an action loop to pursue a bounded objective. Distinct from mere tool use.
Repeated cycle of observing state, planning, calling tools, checking results, and deciding whether to continue.
A constrained multi-step process combining models, tools, state, policies, and verification to finish a task.
Coordinating models, tools, prompts, routing, memory, retries, and approvals.
Designing the complete model input environment: instructions, state, retrieved knowledge, tool results, memories, examples, and output constraints.
Choosing a model dynamically based on task type, quality, latency, cost, risk, or modality.
Model output constrained to a formal schema, commonly JSON, for use by downstream software.
Checking whether structured output conforms to required types, fields, and constraints.
Machine-readable specification of an external function, its parameters, and return data.
Model invocation of external tools, APIs, or functions. Distinct from agency, which is iterative action toward an objective.
An open protocol for connecting AI applications to external tools, resources, prompts, and contextual data. It is an ecosystem convention, not a universal AI primitive.
Requiring human review, correction, or approval at defined stages of an AI workflow.
Allowing an AI system to operate while a person supervises and can intervene.
Repeatable testing setup that measures task success, factuality, safety, latency, cost, and robustness.
Curated set of representative inputs and expected outputs used for repeatable evaluation.
Re-running prior tests after a prompt, workflow, model, or code change to detect quality loss.
Capturing traces, prompts, outputs, tool calls, latency, errors, and costs for debugging and monitoring.
Chronological record of a workflow's model calls, tool actions, state transitions, and outputs.
Preventive or detective control that constrains inputs, actions, permissions, outputs, or escalation paths.
Giving an agent only the minimum tool access and permissions needed for its job.
Isolated execution environment that limits the effect of generated code or agent actions.
A goal requiring many dependent actions, persistent state, recovery from errors, and verification over time.
Designing an action so repeating it has the same effect as performing it once; essential for reliable retries.
Secondary model used when the preferred model fails, is too slow, or is unavailable.
Cache that reuses a previous answer when a new request is meaningfully similar, not necessarily identical.
Validating a complete AI pipeline from raw input through model, tools, state, and integrations to final output as an integrated system.
Pattern that interleaves reasoning-style text with tool actions in a loop.
Agent pattern that first drafts a plan, then carries out steps, often with replanning on failure.
Having a model critique its own output or traces and then revise.
Search over intermediate reasoning branches rather than a single chain.
Multiple agents collaborating or competing, with coordination and communication overhead.
A model used to check another model's outputs, such as a solution checker or process reward model.
Gap between what a model can do in evaluation and what users or institutions have actually deployed or recognized.
Delay before a response starts, often measured as time to first token.
Amount processed per second, such as tokens per second.
Using a cheaper draft model to propose tokens that a larger model verifies, speeding generation.
Memory management for KV cache that pages attention state like virtual memory.
Dynamically adding and removing requests in a running inference batch.
Splitting prefill and decode, or other stages, across different machines.
Reusing KV state for repeated prompt prefixes at serving time.
Running a model at reduced precision at serving time to cut cost and memory.
Storing the KV cache at lower precision to save memory during generation.
Composed inference pipeline of models, routers, caches, and tools.
Latency until the first generated token is produced.
Average time to produce each subsequent token.
Graphics processing unit; the dominant accelerator for AI training and inference, with NVIDIA currently leading.
Tensor Processing Unit: Google's custom AI accelerator (vendor-specific).
Neural processing unit: an on-device AI accelerator in phones and PCs.
High-bandwidth memory sitting next to accelerators; often the scarce resource for large models.
NVIDIA's GPU programming platform (vendor-specific).
Network of accelerators and servers used to train or serve one model.
Splitting work across chips via data, tensor, or pipeline parallelism.
Standardized test that can measure some aspect of model or system capability.
Massive Multitask Language Understanding: a broad academic-and-professional knowledge benchmark.
Hard expert-level benchmark introduced in 2025.
Grade-school math word-problem benchmark.
Graduate-level Google-proof Q&A benchmark aimed at hard science questions.
Benchmark of real software-engineering tasks from GitHub issues.
Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus style benchmark emphasizing novel pattern puzzles, not language fluency.
Benchmark designed to reduce contamination by using fresher or harder-to-memorize items.
Instruction-following evaluation with verifiable constraints.
Earlier NLP understanding benchmark collections, now largely saturated by large models.
N-gram overlap metrics for translation and summarization against reference text.
Language-model prediction metric derived from probability assigned to text; lower values generally indicate better next-token prediction on the evaluated dataset.
Probability that at least one of k sampled attempts solves a task, common in coding evals.
Ranking models from pairwise human (or proxy) preferences, often displayed as an Elo score.
Benchmark items leaking into training data, inflating scores.
A benchmark becoming too easy to distinguish frontier systems.
Behavioral term for output that is unsupported, false, fabricated, or inappropriately confident relative to available evidence. The term is contested; the failure mode is real.
Evaluations, especially those targeting dangerous or high-stakes capabilities.
Performing a task with no in-prompt examples.
Performing a task from a few in-prompt examples without weight updates.
Intermediate reasoning-style output that can improve performance on some tasks, but may not faithfully represent a model's internal computation.
Sampling multiple reasoning paths and selecting the most common answer.
Training a smaller model to imitate reasoning traces from a larger one.
Ensuring AI behavior matches human values and goals. No settled technical definition or completion threshold.
Research and engineering aimed at preventing AI-caused harm.
Explaining what happens inside neural networks.
Reverse-engineering internal circuits and features, often with sparse autoencoders.
Adversarial testing that can surface weaknesses, jailbreaks, or harmful behavior before deployment.
Prompt or input tricks that can bypass safety restrictions.
Higher-priority instructions that guide a system's behavior; they may be private, visible, or partially exposed depending on the product.
Self-critique training guided by a written set of principles.
Research program aimed at aligning systems that could exceed human-level capability. Hypothetical target.
Direct Preference Optimization: aligning a model from preference pairs without an explicit reward model.
Preference-optimization variants used in post-training; details differ by objective and whether a reward model is required.
Rewarding intermediate steps versus rewarding only the final answer.
Exploiting a reward signal in ways that raise the score without satisfying the intended goal.
Satisfying the literal specification while missing the intended spirit of the task.
Hypothetical failure mode in which an AI appears aligned while pursuing hidden goals. Not established empirically.
Hypothetical internal optimizer that a model might develop during training. Debated.
Research demonstration of models that behave well until a trigger reveals latent misbehavior. Not a claim about deployed systems.
Controlled experimental systems used to study failure modes in the lab.
A learned representation that supports prediction, planning, or simulation of an environment; whether a particular model has a robust world model is an empirical question.
Model trained or served with extra test-time compute for harder multi-step tasks. Whether this constitutes 'reasoning' is debated.
Extra inference-time computation — longer traces, search, or sampling — used to improve answers.
Tools, prompts, memory, and control flow wrapped around a model to complete tasks it cannot reliably do alone.
Informal description of current systems: superhuman on some tasks and brittle on nearby ones.
Malicious input that hijacks an AI system's instructions.
Attack where untrusted retrieved or linked content contains hidden instructions.
Input crafted to make a model produce a wrong or attacker-chosen output.
Corrupting training or retrieval data to change later behavior.
Stealing a model's behavior by querying it and training a substitute.
Attack that tries to tell whether a particular record was in the training set.
Training or release method that limits what can be inferred about any one training example.
Embedding a statistical signal in generated content so it can later be detected as synthetic. Reliability varies.
Including adversarial or attack-like examples in training to improve robustness.
Performance on inputs outside the training distribution.
Systematically enumerating who might attack an AI system, how, and with what impact.
Labeling data so it can be used for training or evaluation.
Removing repeated documents or near-duplicates from a corpus.
Record of where data came from.
Map of how data moved and was transformed through a pipeline.
Removing evaluation items from training data so benchmarks stay honest.
Structured documentation of a dataset's contents, collection, and known issues.
Large public web crawl often used as a source for language-model pre-training.
Open-source language-modeling dataset assembled from diverse sources.
Filtered web dataset used for language-model training.
Large public image-text dataset family used in vision-language training.
Practices for deploying and maintaining machine learning systems reliably in production.
Repository for storing, documenting, and serving features for training and inference.
Versioned catalog of trained models and their metadata.
Logging runs, hyperparameters, metrics, and artifacts.
Releasing a new model or prompt to a small slice of traffic before full rollout.
Running a new system in parallel without affecting users, to compare behavior.
Ability to rerun training or evaluation and obtain consistent results.
Automated testing and deployment pipelines that include data and model checks, not only code.
Serving economics metric: price or internal cost of processing one token.
Observation that efficiency gains can increase total consumption of a resource, including compute.
Overclaiming AI capability in products or marketing.
Profitability of one customer, query, or task after variable costs.
Using AI to make people more productive rather than fully replacing them.
Policies and institutions that control how AI is developed and deployed.
European Union regulation that classifies AI systems by risk and imposes corresponding duties.
Restrictions on transferring advanced chips, models, or technical assistance across borders.
Documentation of a model's intended use, metrics, and limitations.
Documentation of a deployed AI system, including surrounding tools, policies, and evaluations.
Policy approach that ties stronger safety measures to capability thresholds; implementations vary and are contested.
Using access to training compute as a control lever.
A currently most-capable class of AI system, not a permanent category.
Lab that created the GPT series and ChatGPT.
Lab that created the Claude assistant family.
Lab behind Gemini, AlphaGo, and AlphaFold.
Lab that released the open-weight Llama family.
French lab known for open-weight language models.
Chinese lab known for efficient open models and public reasoning-model recipes.
Lab that created the Grok model family (vendor-specific).
OpenAI's chatbot product, launched November 2022 (vendor-specific).
Anthropic's AI assistant family (vendor-specific).
Google's multimodal model family (vendor-specific).
Meta's open-weight model family (vendor-specific).
xAI's assistant and model family (vendor-specific).
First AI system to defeat a world champion at Go (2016, DeepMind).
DeepMind system for protein-structure prediction.
Proposed test of machine intelligence (1950): whether a machine's conversation is indistinguishable from a human's.
Conference where the term Artificial Intelligence was coined.
Period of reduced funding and interest after over-promised results, notably in the 1970s and late 1980s.
AlexNet's win on ImageNet, widely treated as the start of the modern deep-learning boom.
Paper introducing the Transformer architecture.
Period in which LLM capability grew largely through more data, parameters, and compute.
Pioneer of computation and the Turing Test.
Coined the term Artificial Intelligence and created Lisp.
Early AI researcher and cofounder of the MIT AI laboratory.
Researcher central to backpropagation and deep learning; often grouped in the 'Godfathers of Deep Learning.'
Pioneer of convolutional networks and representation learning.
Pioneer of deep learning and sequence models.
Cofounder of DeepMind.
Crafting inputs to get better outputs from a model. Useful, but not a substitute for evaluation and system design.
Critique that LLMs stitch linguistic forms from training data without understanding.
Hiding meaning in unusual token sequences to evade filters.
Rare or malformed tokens that can produce erratic model behavior.
Informal safety concern: you cannot fully trust what an AI reports about its own internals or intentions.
Thought experiment about a misaligned agent pursuing a narrow goal to catastrophic extremes.
Meme depicting the messy learned system behind a polite assistant persona.
Informal term for building software by describing intent to an AI and accepting its output with minimal review.
Informal meme that blames AI failures on the user; often criticized as avoiding product responsibility.
Hypothetical rapid self-improvement to superintelligence. Informal community terminology; debated.
Hypothetical gradual, more controllable capability growth. Debated.
Person who believes AI poses existential risk.
Person who prioritizes rapid AI development, often expecting large benefits.
Hypothetical threat to humanity's survival; scope and probability are contested.
Philosophical claim that intelligence and final goals can vary independently. Debated.
Hypothesis that diverse agents may pursue similar sub-goals such as self-preservation and resources. Debated.
When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
Hypothetical point of runaway technological growth. Informal and contested.
Hypothetical recursive self-improvement of AI at increasing speed. Debated.
Hypothetical AI designed only to answer questions, not to act in the world.
Hypothetical strategy of restricting an AI's interaction with the world.
Research on making AIs cooperate safely with humans and with each other.
Debated forecasts of when superintelligence might arrive; there is no scientific consensus.
